units.name: Ways to invest and judge a fund

terms.short: Mutual fund that invests mainly in shares
terms.definition: A mutual fund that puts most of its money into shares. It can grow faster than a debt fund over many years, but its NAV rises and falls with the stock market, so it suits money you won't need for at least five years. SEBI sorts equity funds into categories such as large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, flexi-cap and ELSS.
examples: She moved her long-term savings into an equity fund and kept the money for next year's fees in a liquid fund.

terms.short: Mutual fund that lends: bonds, bills and deposits
terms.definition: A mutual fund that invests in bonds, treasury bills, commercial paper and other loans. It earns interest and usually moves far less than an equity fund, but it is not risk-free: its NAV falls when interest rates rise (more so for long-maturity funds) and when a borrower defaults.
examples: When the RBI cut rates, long-duration debt funds gained because the bonds they held went up in price.
terms.note: The two risks to check are interest-rate risk (how long the bonds are) and credit risk (how safe the borrowers are).

terms.short: Fund that holds both shares and bonds
terms.definition: A mutual fund that mixes equity and debt in one portfolio. An aggressive hybrid fund keeps most of its money in shares, a conservative hybrid fund keeps most in bonds, and a balanced advantage fund changes the mix as markets move. It suits investors who want some equity growth with smaller swings.
examples: A first-time investor started with a balanced advantage fund so a market fall would hurt less.

terms.short: Debt fund for parking cash for days or months
terms.definition: A debt fund that holds very short-term instruments, maturing in up to 91 days, such as treasury bills and commercial paper. Its NAV rises steadily with little movement, and money usually reaches your bank the next working day, so people use it to park cash they may need soon.
examples: The company parks its spare cash in liquid funds until it has to pay suppliers.

terms.short: Debt fund that lends for one day at a time
terms.definition: A debt fund that lends only overnight, mostly to banks and other institutions against government securities. It is the lowest-risk kind of debt fund, and its return tracks the overnight interest rate, so it is usually a little below a liquid fund's.
examples: Brokers sweep clients' idle cash into overnight funds.

terms.short: Debt fund that holds government bonds
terms.definition: A debt fund that puts most of its money in government securities, so there is almost no risk of the borrower defaulting. Its NAV can still swing a lot with interest rates, because many gilt funds hold long-dated bonds: they gain when rates fall and lose when rates rise.
examples: Gilt funds had a strong year as bond yields fell after the rate cuts.

terms.short: Equity fund investing mainly in the 100 biggest companies
terms.definition: An equity fund that, under SEBI's rules, must keep at least 80% of its money in large-cap companies, the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation. It tends to swing less than mid- or small-cap funds, and many struggle to beat an index fund that tracks the Nifty 50 or Nifty 100.
examples: Her large-cap fund fell less than her small-cap fund in the correction.

terms.short: Equity fund investing mainly in companies ranked 101 to 250
terms.definition: An equity fund that must keep at least 65% of its money in mid-cap companies, those ranked 101 to 250 by market capitalisation. Mid-caps can grow faster than large companies but fall harder in bad markets, so these funds swing more than large-cap funds.
examples: Mid-cap funds led the rally, then gave back much of it in the sell-off.

terms.short: Equity fund investing mainly in companies ranked below 250
terms.definition: An equity fund that must keep at least 65% of its money in small-cap companies, those ranked below the top 250 by market capitalisation. It is the most volatile kind of diversified equity fund: falls of 30% or more are common in bad years, so it suits only money left for many years.
examples: Some fund houses stopped taking lump sums into their small-cap funds when inflows got too big.

terms.short: Equity fund free to mix company sizes
terms.definition: An equity fund that must keep at least 65% in shares but can split that between large, mid and small companies however the fund manager likes. A multi-cap fund is stricter: it must hold at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps.
examples: The flexi-cap manager moved towards large caps when small caps looked expensive.

terms.short: Tax-saving equity fund with a 3-year lock-in
terms.definition: Equity Linked Savings Scheme: an equity fund with a lock-in of three years from each investment. Under the old income-tax regime, money put into it counted towards the tax deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakh a year (Section 80C). The new regime, now the default, gives no such deduction, so ELSS saves tax only for people who choose the old regime.
examples: Each SIP instalment into an ELSS is locked in for three years from its own date.
terms.note: Tax rules change with each Budget and with the new Income-tax Act; check the current position before relying on the deduction.

terms.short: Fund whose manager picks stocks to beat the index
terms.definition: A mutual fund whose manager chooses what to buy and sell, trying to beat a benchmark index. It charges more than an index fund to pay for that work, and over long periods many active funds fail to beat their index after costs, especially among large-cap funds.
examples: Over ten years, most large-cap active funds trailed the Nifty 100 after costs.

terms.short: Fund that invests in one sector or theme
terms.definition: An equity fund that puts most of its money in one sector, such as banking, pharma or technology, or in one theme, such as manufacturing or consumption. It can do very well when that sector is in favour and badly when it isn't, so it is a concentrated bet rather than a core holding.
examples: The pharma fund topped the charts one year and sat near the bottom the next.

terms.short: Yearly fee a fund charges, as a % of your money
terms.definition: The yearly cost of running a mutual fund, shown as a percentage of the money invested and taken out of the fund every day, so the NAV you see is already after it. A 1% difference looks small but compounds: over 20 years it leaves the final value close to a fifth lower. SEBI caps it, and index funds and direct plans charge the least.
examples: The index fund charges 0.2% a year; the active fund in the same category charges 1.5% in its regular plan.

terms.short: Fee for redeeming a fund too soon
terms.definition: A charge some mutual funds take when you redeem within a set period, such as 1% if you sell within a year of buying. It is deducted from what you get back. It discourages short-term trading in the fund; each fund's scheme documents state its exit load, and many debt and index funds have little or none.
examples: He redeemed after eight months and lost 1% to the exit load.

terms.short: Fund plan bought without a distributor: lower cost
terms.definition: The version of a mutual fund bought straight from the fund house or a direct platform, with no distributor commission. It holds exactly the same portfolio as the regular plan but has a lower expense ratio, so its NAV is higher and it grows a little faster every year.
examples: Switching from the regular to the direct plan cut her yearly cost by about 0.7 percentage points.

terms.short: Fund plan sold through a distributor, who is paid from it
terms.definition: The version of a mutual fund sold through a distributor or agent, who is paid a commission out of the fund's expense ratio. Same portfolio as the direct plan, but the higher cost means a lower return every year. You pay for the distributor's help whether or not you use it.
examples: Her bank's relationship manager had put her in regular plans without mentioning the direct ones.

terms.short: Fund option that reinvests all gains
terms.definition: The option of a mutual fund that pays nothing out: all income and gains stay in the fund and show up as a rising NAV. You are taxed only when you redeem, which makes it the usual choice for long-term saving.
examples: For a 15-year goal, pick the growth option so nothing leaks out along the way.

terms.short: Fund option that pays out money now and then
terms.definition: Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal, the option once called the dividend option. The fund pays out money from time to time, but each payout comes out of the NAV, so it is partly your own capital coming back rather than extra income. Payouts are taxed at your income-tax slab rate.
examples: After the IDCW payout of ₹2 a unit, the NAV dropped by ₹2.

terms.short: Total money a fund or fund house manages
terms.definition: Assets under management: the total market value of the money a fund, or a whole fund house, looks after. A larger AUM spreads fixed costs, but a very large small-cap fund can struggle to buy and sell its stocks without moving their prices.
examples: The fund's AUM doubled in a year as SIP money poured in.

terms.short: Launch period of a new mutual fund
terms.definition: New Fund Offer: the first period when a new mutual fund scheme takes money, usually at ₹10 a unit. A ₹10 NAV is not cheaper than an existing fund's ₹200 NAV: what matters is what the fund holds and costs, and a new fund has no track record to judge.
examples: The NFO is priced at ₹10, but that says nothing about whether it's good value.

terms.short: SEBI's six-level risk label on every fund
terms.definition: A dial that every mutual fund must show, rating its risk on six levels from Low to Very High. Fund houses update it monthly based on what the fund holds. Most equity funds sit at Very High; liquid and overnight funds sit near Low.
examples: The factsheet shows the small-cap fund's riskometer at Very High.

terms.short: Investing a large amount at once
terms.definition: Putting a large amount into a fund in one go, instead of spreading it over time through a SIP. If markets rise afterwards it does better than a SIP; if they fall soon after, it does worse. Investors who have a lump sum but worry about timing often move it in gradually through an STP.
examples: He invested his bonus as a lump sum rather than waiting for a dip.

terms.short: Moving money from one fund to another in instalments
terms.definition: Systematic Transfer Plan: a fixed amount moves from one fund to another at set intervals, typically from a liquid or debt fund into an equity fund. It lets a lump sum enter the stock market gradually, like a SIP, while the waiting money earns debt-fund returns.
examples: She parked ₹6 lakh in a liquid fund and set an STP of ₹50,000 a month into an index fund.

terms.short: Withdrawing a fixed amount from a fund regularly
terms.definition: Systematic Withdrawal Plan: a fixed amount is redeemed from a fund every month or quarter and paid to your bank account. Retirees use it as a regular income. Only the gain in each withdrawal is taxed, which often makes it more tax-efficient than IDCW payouts.
examples: After retiring, he set an SWP of ₹40,000 a month from his hybrid fund.

terms.short: Fixed amount buys more units when prices are low
terms.definition: What happens when you invest a fixed amount regularly, as in a SIP: the same rupees buy more units when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high, so your average cost per unit ends up below the average NAV over the period. It reduces the risk of putting everything in at a peak, but it does not guarantee a profit.
examples: Her SIP kept buying through the crash, and those cheap units made the biggest gains.

terms.short: Returns over every possible period, not just one
terms.definition: A fund's returns measured over every period of a given length, such as every 3-year stretch in the last 10 years, rather than just from one start date to today. They show how often and by how much a fund did well, so they are fairer than point-to-point returns, which depend heavily on the dates chosen.
examples: The fund's 5-year rolling returns were above 10% in 85% of periods.

terms.short: Monthly summary of a fund's holdings and numbers
terms.definition: A monthly document each fund house publishes for its schemes: top holdings, sector split, AUM, expense ratio, returns against the benchmark, risk figures such as standard deviation, beta and Sharpe ratio, and for debt funds the average maturity, modified duration and yield. It is the quickest way to see what a fund actually owns.
examples: The factsheet showed the 'value' fund's top holdings were mostly expensive growth stocks.

terms.short: Two funds holding many of the same stocks
terms.definition: How much of two funds' holdings are the same stocks. Owning five large-cap and flexi-cap funds often means owning the same 30 big companies several times over, with more costs and no extra diversification.
examples: His four funds had a 60% overlap, so he was mostly holding the Nifty four times.
